title: The Unity of the Divine Hypostases
english: Will anyone know Him? Instead of 'no one'. Regarding the divine: 'Who will explain His generation, since His life is taken from the earth?' The generation is the begetting, the life is existence, and the phrase 'taken from the earth' is a most mystical way of calling Him one who transcends immeasurably from the earth and surpasses every mind.

For because He has become everything to all, He is one whom anyone, having circled much with the intellect through all time, finds to be infinitely highest, incomparably better in quantity than all, unsearchable in essence, and everywhere inaccessible—having enveloped Himself and having nothing of Himself outside. Even the multitude of angels and the whole host of heavenly ranks cry out in this way: David in Psalm 18 says, 'He set darkness as His secret covering and His tabernacle around Him'; and Habakkuk says, 'His excellence covered the heavens'; and Matthew says, 'no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son' (Matt 11:27).

For that which is born of creation through the union of one with another is not of the same nature as the begetter, nor does it emerge immediately and impassively perfect. Regarding divinity, the same applies. Since creation is such, the creator is the opposite of His own works, not similar to them, as only the blessed Trinity knows this.

For if He were not incomprehensible, He would be grasped; nor a mystery, if He were known; nor divine, if He could be reached; nor the creator of all, if He were from time; nor uncomposed and undivided, if He were in relation to bodies.

Just as those hearing about the Father say, 'You are from age to age' (Ps 90:2) and 'Your truth is unto the clouds' (Psalm 36:5), we do not set limits upon Him, but believe in His eternity; for the age does not dwell with Him. We ought to think the same regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit, because of the one prevailing nature into which these blessed hypostases exist.

The same melody applies to the Son: 'You are the same, and your years will not fail' (Ps 102:27). And although what is written of the Father is small, 'who is from the ages' (Psalm 55:19), what is said of His Son is not small, that He is 'the eternal God'. It is clear He is unsearchable, as will be shown shortly. And just as the Father...

Not merely 'immortality', but rather He is immortality itself; in this same way the Son is 'eternal life', and is the very same thing. Just as the Father is said to be 'one God', so the Son is called monogenes, God, Word, and 'one Lord Jesus Christ'.

And just as James writes concerning Him, 'there is one lawgiver and judge, able alone to save' (James 4:12), so the Spirit, according to the hymns written by Paul to the Corinthians and Ephesians, is called 'one' and 'the same' and 'only'; so that by this numerical expression, as it is said, these blessed hypostases demonstrate the single or unique nature of the Father's deity. And if 'the God and Lord' is true of the Father, it is without falsehood also of His Son and of the Spirit.

For as we have often recalled, the older Testament, having preserved equal value, has spoken: 'The Lord said to my Lord' (Psalm 110:1), and 'The Lord rained down from the Lord', and 'God made man in the image of God' (Genesis 1:26), and 'Who is a God beside the Lord, and who is a God besides our God?'. And in the New Testament, John said what has already been said; Thomas [said], 'My Lord and my God' (John 20:28); and Paul [said], 'the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty' (2 Corinthians 3:17), and again, 'as from the Lord Spirit' and 'may the Lord find grace for Onesiphorus's house'. And Job [said]: 'A divine spirit made me', and 'a divine spirit surrounds me with rays'.

It is the same in Scripture to say 'divine' or 'God', as Paul teaches the Romans: 'His eternal power and deity' (Romans 1:20); and the Acts [say]: 'we ought not to suppose that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, or an artifice of human thought' (Acts 17:29); and Peter in the second epistle: 'that you might become partakers of the divine nature' (2 Peter 1:4).

And in whatever way the Father is incomprehensible, so also the riches of the Christ, according to Paul, turn out to be unsearchable. For he says: 'To me, the least of all men, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ' (Ephesians 3:8). But also 'there is no end to His greatness' and neither 'is there a number to His wisdom' according to David, nor 'a limit to His peace' according to Isaiah.

title: The Unoriginate Hypostases
english: “And your incorruptible spirit,” he says, “is in all things” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:1), and “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:7). For no one would be found so dull and slow of mind as not to see, from these unfeigned and pure testimonies, the boundlessness of the Only-begotten and of the all-holy Spirit.

And I say that what the Apostle wrote about both hypostases is of equal weight and in like words: what he says of the Father, “God, who is over all and through all and in all” (Ephesians 4:6), and “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, knows that I do not lie” (2 Corinthians 11:31); and what he wrote to the Romans of the Son, “who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Romans 9:5). Besides this there is also “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1:23).

Again, what is declared of the Father is alike, “that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28), and of his Son, “where there is neither Greek nor Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all in all” (Colossians 3:11); and elsewhere, “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and things on earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is one Lord” (Philippians 2:10-11).

As for the Spirit, both by what was said of him just now and because all that the Father is must be understood of him too, as his Spirit, except for being Father. For he images God both in this and in all things, as it declares: “By this we know that he is in us, from his Spirit, which he has given us” (1 John 3:24).

And of equal force with what was sung of God the Father, “You alone are Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 83:18), is what was spoken in prophecy of the Son in the eighty-seventh Psalm, “Mother Zion will say: A man, and a man was born in it, and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 87:5), and what was said of the Holy Spirit in the Gospel, “You will receive power from on high when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8).

And just as the Father is great, among other things, because he knows the Son, so the Son too is great because he knows the Father; and likewise the Holy Spirit, for it says, “So too no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11). And no different from what Paul wrote to the Hebrews about the Father, “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things” (Hebrews 2:10), is what was spoken in prophecy about the Son, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), and about the Spirit, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6).

So these glorious hypostases, honoured equally with God the Father, as having received for their portion his divine nature, which is over all, unmixed and beyond compare: how could they be counted among all things under God, as those who vote them creatures would have it?

For just as it is impossible that the Father should not be Father without beginning and in truth (for he did not get this name in time, nor as an added title), so it is impossible that the Son, the Word, and his Spirit should not be without beginning and by nature from his hypostasis. For at once with his being Father (let me be pardoned for putting it so), without any interval the one was begotten and the other proceeded.

So he has not been deprived of being Father of the Only-begotten and of having his Spirit proceeding from him. And because he is Father, he does not differ from the Son and his Spirit either in time or in substance. For if he had begotten later, he would have been changed or altered, which is foreign to the Godhead; and besides, God would be found at some time not called Father, or not being Father, as not yet having begotten.

And the Apostle, setting before the Hebrews how the generation of the Son of God is without beginning and beyond comprehension, writes of Melchizedek: “Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, made like the Son of God” (Hebrews 7:3).

He had been made like him (in that he was not given a genealogy, as it was the custom to do in the tribes of Israel for those held in honour among them) because he is a type and a kind of outline of the Lord, who above is without mother and without time, and below is without father and in time.

And yet Melchizedek was a notable priest, so that Abraham was blessed by him and gave him tithes of the spoils, as the same Apostle says: “Consider how great this man is, to whom Abraham gave a tenth of everything” (Hebrews 7:4). And again: “And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, has paid tithes” (Hebrews 7:9), that is, through his forefather Abraham. “For he was still,” he says, “in the loins of his father” (Hebrews 7:10): Levi, the descendant of Abraham, from whom the …

title: The Creator and Center of All
english: The meeting with the Lord was thought of generally—that is, with Abraham—the Melchizedek. What then is the will of their empty-headedness and how is it absurd? For they say whoever wishes to call [Him] the Beginning, and confess the end, and promise to the generation, and accept death from this [generation]; and they suppose that which comes from non-existence or from the dissimilarity of the divine essence to have become mortal and at the same time foreign to the composition of the Father, which is merely said, not even honored, as a mediator of all ungodliness.

But are their things then strong against the 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1)? It was written also concerning creation, he says, the 'was'. For it has 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth, and the earth was formless and void' (Gen 1:1-2), and 'there was a man of Ramathaim-Ziphah' (1 Samuel 1:1). There is nothing common to the 'In the beginning was' and the 'In the beginning God made', nor to the creator in relation to the creation. For the 'was' concerning the creation is said and believed only regarding the flowing and passing time.

For the creation was after the non-existent came to be. For he said in advance that He made it, and then he added the 'was', so that it might not be thought automatic. But concerning the God the Word, it signifies the super-beginning. For 'In the beginning', he says, 'was' and 'was God' (John 1:1), and the 'In the beginning was' pushes out from non-existence.

But they testify concerning the being of the Son as eternal and maker of the ages thus: Paul, writing to the Hebrews: 'Long ago God, speaking in many parts and many ways, to the fathers by the prophets, in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages' (Heb 1:1-2); so he inherits his own things both as maker of them and as true Son; and he was appointed heir as having become man. And to the Corinthians in the first epistle: 'For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1 Cor 3:11), that is, it is impossible for a beginning of the Son to be devised. 'For in him and through him' is every beginning.
And David in the 84th psalm, singing about the ruler: 'Our God, the eternal King, worked salvation in the midst of the earth' (Psalm 74:12). And he says the Golgotha, the middle place and such like.

A center which names him under heaven; in whom, by his divine foreknowledge, the Son worked out salvation for us through the incarnation, and in fact, when the impassible one suffered through goodness as he knew and willed for our sake, and reached, as they say, 'to the heart of the earth' (Ezekiel 28:26: 'I have set her, Jerusalem, in the midst of the nations'). And in the 119th Psalm: 'Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven' (Psalm 119:89). And the Lord himself, utterly excluding the heretics, said concerning himself: 'Amen, amen, I say to you, before the ages were, I am' (John 8:58).

Regarding the establishing of all things as creator, both incorporeal and corporeal, but not as subordinate or mediator, and in this also as without beginning, according to the testimonies already set forth; and David in the 33rd Psalm sings: 'Our God in heaven and on earth did all that he willed' (Psalm 115:3). He did not say: 'all that was permitted.'

Who then would deny that the self-determining and all-determining Monad exists, the one who acts by his own will and has all things rushing together by his pure, intrinsic breath, without necessity? And in the 89th Psalm: 'You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain. And all of them will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail' (Psalm 102:25), instead of 'you are without beginning and without end.'

And Paul writes the same to the Ephesians: 'in God who created all things' (Ephesians 3:9), and to the Colossians: 'because in him all things were created, those in the heavens and those on the earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and for him, and he is before all things, and in him all things consist' (Colossians 1:16-17). For he who essentially depicts God and the one before all things in divinity, no one surpasses or is elder than him, just as no one is subject to or later than the one who is after all things.
And in another way: if he is before all things, alone from alone and by alone, absolutely generated before every activity, and is essentially the Son of the Father. For it is necessary...
